extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, educators, and policymakers interested in public opinion, civic education, and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and practical guidance for understanding how people's internal 'pictures' (pseudo-environments) shape political behavior, and how education, intelligence work, and journalism can correct or reinforce those pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beliefs must correspond to the real environment
rubrics_metrics.description: What each man does is based not on direct and certain knowledge, but on pictures made by himself or given to him; the way in which the world is imagined determines at any particular moment what men will do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether popular or political beliefs correspond to actual conditions; be aware that acting on inaccurate pictures produces maladjustment ("butting one's head against a stone wall"). Examples: the months in 1914 when people continued ordinary business despite the coming war; senators reacting to an erroneous cable about marines in the Adriatic. The analyst should seek to compare people’s pictures with the real environment and note consequences when they diverge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and analyze the pseudo-environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The insertion between man and his environment of a pseudo-environment: to that pseudo-environment his behavior is a response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the 'pseudo-environment' as a core analytic object: identify the images, symbols, and schemata through which groups perceive distant or complex events. Map how these pseudo-environments are constructed (reports, traditions, propaganda, superstition) and trace how they drive emotions and actions distinct from the real environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess source provenance and reporter credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach the habit of examining the sources of information: look in the newspaper for the place where the dispatch was filed, for the name of the correspondent, the name of the press service, the authority given for the statement, the circumstances under which the statement was secured; ask whether the reporter saw what he describes, and remember how that reporter described other events in the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a news item, systematically check dispatch origin, correspondent, press service, cited authorities, eyewitness status, and reporter track record; factor in censorship and past propaganda. Use these checks as routine critical practice in civic education and analysis to reduce credulity and partisan manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic intelligence and social data gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: The gathering of social knowledge is, on the whole, still haphazard; not, as it will have to become, the normal accompaniment of action. The collection of information will not be made ... for the sake of its ultimate use. It will be made because modern decision requires it to be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should develop routine intelligence practices so decision-makers have valid pictures of relevant environments. Analysts and critics depend on expert reporters and intelligence work to provide reliable environmental descriptions; without them, dialectical critique is limited. Encourage systematic, institutionalized data collection as a precondition of sound public decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use schematic models/fictions but account for their fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: By fictions I do not mean lies. I mean a representation of the environment which is in lesser or greater degree made by man himself. The range of fiction extends all the way from complete hallucination to the scientists' perfectly self-conscious use of a schematic model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that models and simplified 'fictions' are necessary for thought and action, but always keep their degree of fidelity explicit. Specify assumptions and limits of models; account for where stylization or simplification may mislead; treat models as instruments whose usefulness depends on known approximation errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach metacognitive awareness of imagery, stereotypes, and dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher can ... furnish him with knowledge of past propaganda. He can, by the proper use of history, make him aware of the stereotype, and can educate a habit of introspection about the imagery evoked by printed words. He can teach men to catch themselves making allegories, dramatizing relations, and personifying abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic education should train pupils to notice how language evokes images and stereotypes, to identify allegorizing and personification, and to examine their own mental images. Use history and anthropology to expose cultural codes that shape perception, and practice case-method exercises to build self-awareness about how one forms opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case method, comparative history and anthropology in civic education
rubrics_metrics.description: As a working model of the social system becomes available to the teacher, he can use it to make the pupil acutely aware of how his mind works on unfamiliar facts. ... By the proper use of history ... by courses in comparative history and anthropology, produce a life-long realization of the way codes impose a special pattern upon the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concrete case studies, comparative history, and anthropological perspectives in curricula to teach students to analyze sources, recognize codes and stereotypes, and understand the construction of public images. Emphasize study of error as a pedagogical tool that motivates appreciation for objective method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the time-differential in political reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a time-differential ... the rate at which reason, as we possess it, can advance itself is slower than the rate at which action has to be taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing policies or critiques, explicitly consider the length of time operations require and whether the data or conditions assumed will remain stable. Distinguish short-term emergencies (where quick, non-rational measures may be necessary) from long-term planning (where reasoned, evidence-based approaches can be instituted). Reason is more practicable where there is stability and time for education and institutional adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits of appeal to reason during crises
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an inherent difficulty about using the method of reason to deal with an unreasoning world. In the crisis, the only advice is to use a gun, or make a speech, utter a stirring slogan, offer a compromise, employ any quick means available to quell the mutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that in emergencies there may be no time to educate or persuade by slow rational methods; decision-makers must often resort to immediate practical means. Design institutions and preparations on shore (long-term) to reduce reliance on such expedients in future crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for symbolic pictures and personified leaders/enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost the whole of each party believes absolutely in its picture of the opposition ... Great men ... are usually known to the public only through a fictitious personality. The ideal Joffre ... incarnated for the conscience of mankind the victory of good over evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how hero-worship, demonization, and personification compress complex events into symbolic figures; examine how these symbols mobilize emotion and behavior. When assessing public opinion, identify dominant symbols, how they were formed, and how they may sustain or mislead collective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the triangular relationship: scene, picture, response
rubrics_metrics.description: The analyst of public opinion must begin then, by recognizing the triangular relationship between the scene of action, the human picture of that scene, and the human response to that picture working itself out upon the scene of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure analysis around: (1) the actual situation (scene), (2) the mental representation held by actors (picture), and (3) the behavior produced (response). Use this framework to trace causal paths, identify misperceptions, and design interventions to align pictures with facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hatred, intolerance, suspicion, bigotry, secrecy, fear, and lying in appeals to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot prove in every instance that it will, nor why hatred, intolerance, suspicion, bigotry, secrecy, fear, and lying are the seven deadly sins against public opinion. We can only insist that they have no place in the appeal to reason, that in the longer run they are a poison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make avoidance of these behaviors an explicit normative standard in public discourse and civic instruction. Emphasize decency and long-run commitments to openness and truthfulness as preconditions for cultivating reasoned public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide feedback and corrective mechanisms for maladjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: When the stimulus of the pseudo-fact results in action on things or other people, contradiction soon develops. Then comes the sensation of butting one's head against a stone wall ... the discomfort in short of a maladjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutional and educational feedback loops so that when actions based on false pictures meet reality, the errors are detected and corrected: investigations, public reporting, inquiries, and learning practices. Encourage practices that convert experiential contradiction into revised pictures rather than persistent denial.
